# The Coronary Slow Flow Phenomenon: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

The coronary slow flow phenomenon (CSFP) is an angiographic entity characterized by delayed opacification of the distal coronary vasculature in the absence of obstructive epicardial coronary artery disease [1]. First systematically described by Tambe and colleagues in 1972, CSFP has since attracted increasing attention as a cause of recurrent chest pain and a potential contributor to adverse cardiovascular outcomes [2]. Although frequently regarded as a benign incidental finding, accumulating evidence suggests that CSFP is associated with myocardial ischemia, arrhythmias, and impaired quality of life [3].

## Definition and Diagnosis

CSFP is diagnosed angiographically when contrast progresses slowly through coronary arteries that appear otherwise normal or near-normal [1]. The most widely accepted quantitative measure is the corrected Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction (TIMI) frame count (TFC) introduced by Gibson and colleagues, which provides an objective, reproducible index of coronary flow velocity [4]. A TFC exceeding two standard deviations from the normal range for a given vessel is typically used to define slow flow [5]. The TFC has facilitated standardization across studies and improved diagnostic consistency [6].

## Epidemiology

CSFP is identified in approximately 1–7% of patients undergoing coronary angiography for suspected ischemia [7]. It demonstrates a male predominance and tends to affect relatively young patients, often smokers [8]. Many present with recurrent acute coronary syndrome–like episodes, leading to repeated hospital admissions and angiographic procedures [9].

## Pathophysiology

The underlying mechanisms of CSFP remain incompletely understood, and several overlapping hypotheses have been proposed [10]. Microvascular dysfunction is considered central, with evidence of increased microvascular resistance and impaired coronary flow reserve [11]. Endothelial dysfunction, demonstrated through reduced flow-mediated dilation and abnormal nitric oxide bioavailability, has been consistently reported [12]. Histopathological studies have revealed fibromuscular hyperplasia, myointimal proliferation, and endothelial degeneration in small coronary vessels of affected patients [13].

Subclinical diffuse atherosclerosis, detectable by intravascular ultrasound even in angiographically normal segments, has also been implicated [14]. Inflammation appears to play a role, with elevated levels of high-sensitivity C-reactive protein and other inflammatory markers in CSFP patients [15]. Oxidative stress and an imbalance between vasoconstrictor and vasodilator mediators, including elevated endothelin-1 and reduced nitric oxide, further contribute to the abnormal microcirculatory tone [16]. Platelet dysfunction and increased mean platelet volume have likewise been associated with the phenomenon [17].

## Clinical Presentation and Associations

The dominant symptom is recurrent angina, which may occur both at rest and on exertion [18]. CSFP has been linked to abnormal cardiac repolarization, with studies reporting prolonged QT dispersion and an increased propensity for ventricular and atrial arrhythmias [19]. Cases of acute coronary syndrome and even sudden cardiac death attributed to CSFP have been described [20]. Associations with metabolic syndrome, insulin resistance, and obesity have been reported, supporting a systemic vascular component [21]. Elevated serum uric acid, homocysteine, and markers of endothelial activation have also been observed [22].

## Imaging and Functional Assessment

Beyond the TFC, advanced modalities have enhanced understanding of CSFP. Myocardial perfusion imaging may reveal reversible perfusion defects, while echocardiographic measures including tissue Doppler imaging and global longitudinal strain can detect subclinical left ventricular dysfunction [23]. Cardiac magnetic resonance and positron emission tomography offer quantitative assessment of microvascular perfusion abnormalities [24]. Coronary flow reserve measured by Doppler echocardiography is frequently reduced, corroborating microvascular involvement [25].

## Management

There is no universally accepted treatment for CSFP, and management remains largely empirical [26]. Aggressive control of cardiovascular risk factors—particularly smoking cessation—is recommended [8]. Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, especially nifedipine, have shown benefit in reducing symptoms and improving TFC [27]. Dipyridamole and nicorandil, agents that act on the microvasculature, have demonstrated efficacy in small studies [28]. Statins may improve endothelial function and reduce inflammation, with reported improvements in coronary flow [29]. Other agents, including nebivolol and trimetazidine, have shown promise in limited trials [30].

## Prognosis and Future Directions

While CSFP was historically considered benign, evidence now indicates that affected patients experience recurrent symptoms, reduced quality of life, and a measurable burden of major adverse cardiac events [3]. Larger prospective studies and randomized controlled trials are needed to clarify the natural history and to establish evidence-based therapies. Standardized diagnostic criteria and a unified mechanistic framework would substantially advance the field.

## Conclusion

CSFP is an underrecognized but clinically relevant entity rooted in microvascular and endothelial dysfunction. Greater awareness, consistent diagnostic application of the TIMI frame count, and rigorous therapeutic trials are essential to improve outcomes for affected patients.
